section_summary: This section combines public appeals for restricting American exports to Japan with State Department replies explaining why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked and why non-munitions commodities could not legally be embargoed. It also contains diplomatic and military intelligence on Japanese purchases of trucks, aircraft, metals and other strategic supplies, including reports on Italian aircraft deliveries. A major Osaka consular report examines the rapid expansion of Japan’s armament industry and the conversion of small and medium-sized factories to war production.

subfiles.title: Reply to Fred H. Townsend on the Neutrality Act and exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Townsend’s additional views on applying the Neutrality Act and on shipments of scrap iron, cotton and oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges Townsend's May 16 letter, thanks him, and promises careful consideration of his Neutrality Act arguments.

subfiles.title: Eugene Herring’s appeal to President Roosevelt concerning the Far East
subfiles.about: A heavily garbled handwritten appeal asks the President to address American involvement in the Far Eastern crisis.
subfiles.summary: Eugene Herring's May 16 letter to Roosevelt expresses concern about U.S. conduct in the Far East; handwriting mostly illegible.

subfiles.title: Reply to Eugene Herring explaining the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the President had not proclaimed a state of war between China and Japan under the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: State tells Herring a presidential proclamation would stop arms to both China and Japan, no authority exists to bar Japan alone, the statute doesn't cover other commodities, and the President judged invocation contrary to U.S. interests.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Canadian munitions shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a report of the Canadian prime minister’s statement on aircraft and other exports to Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Canada's prime minister said its only shipment to Japan was one aircraft ordered beforehand and exports remain below 1929.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Methodist resolution opposing aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a resolution adopted by the General Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South.
subfiles.summary: Estes transmits the Methodist resolution on instructions from the quadrennial General Conference at Birmingham, with a blessing for the President.

subfiles.title: Methodist resolution against material and financial assistance to Japan
subfiles.from: General Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: Calls for measures preventing American public or private resources from aiding Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: Methodist resolution says Japanese forces invaded China and American materials contribute to its suffering, asking the President and Congress to stop material and financial aid to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Lud H. Estes concerning the Methodist resolution
subfiles.from: Counselor, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the General Conference resolution concerning shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: State notes receipt via the White House of Estes's letter and April 30 resolution and refers him to its May 16 reply.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Military Imports
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Assesses the difficulty of estimating Japanese military imports omitted from official trade statistics.
subfiles.summary: Grew: secrecy laws and removal of metals from trade returns make unrecorded military imports nearly impossible to measure; direct armed-service purchases are excluded, and the embassy is collecting fragments for a later report.

subfiles.title: Richmond boycott advocate’s letter on American supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges Roosevelt to restrict American strategic exports that sustain Japanese aggression and military power.
subfiles.summary: Citing Eliot Janeway's "Japan's Partner," the writer says Japan depends on American oil, steel and nitrates, describes a Richmond boycott, and proposes U.S., British and Dutch coordinated action.

subfiles.title: Report on Japanese automobile imports and military truck orders
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese military commandeering and purchasing of Ford and other trucks for service in China and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Boyce: limited body-building capacity forced the military to commandeer civilian trucks, with more seizures in Hiroshima; thousands operate in North and Central China; a new order of about 2,000 Ford trucks; direct U.S. shipments to Manchukuo exceed Ford's Japanese quota.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Foster Bain’s report on Philippine iron deposits
subfiles.about: Records Bain’s claim that Japanese interests sought to buy 50 million tons from newly identified Philippine iron deposits.
subfiles.summary: Foster Bain says large Philippine iron deposits were found and Japanese interests want to buy 50 million tons, after his recent tour of China, the Philippines, Manchuria and Japan.

subfiles.title: Josh Lee’s forwarding letter to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Forwards constituent correspondence and asks the State Department to comply with its request if possible.
subfiles.summary: Josh Lee forwards a communication for Hull's consideration and asks its return to his Senate office.

subfiles.title: W. C. Sawyer’s direct protest to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Calls for immediate action by the United States and other democracies to stop war supplies reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: W. C. Sawyer condemns Japanese city bombing, says protests alone can't stop it, and asks the U.S. to halt shipments, seek parallel democratic action and notify Japan.

subfiles.title: W. C. Sawyer’s letter to Senator Josh Lee
subfiles.about: Asks Lee to investigate reports of discriminatory war-material shipments and to press for stronger action against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sawyer, after a broadcast on the Hong Kong bombing, says arms allegedly flow to Japan while China's are held up, and asks Lee to present his demand to State.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Senator Josh Lee
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Lee’s referral of Sawyer’s letter and returns it with a copy of the Department’s response.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Lee's June 9 letter enclosing Sawyer's June 4 letter, sends the reply to Sawyer and returns the original.

subfiles.title: Reply to W. C. Sawyer on arms exports to China and Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the Neutrality Act and compares licensed arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: State tells Sawyer it can't stop arms to Japan alone without a war proclamation, which would embargo both; licenses since July 1, 1937 were about $12.68 million for China and $9.29 million for Japan; the President judged invocation not in U.S. interests.

subfiles.title: Harry F. Byrd’s forwarding letter concerning Warren Horton Stuart
subfiles.about: Forwards a former Virginian’s appeal concerning American assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Harry Byrd forwards Professor Warren Stuart's letter from the College of Emporia for the Secretary's consideration.

subfiles.title: Warren Horton Stuart’s appeal against exports and loans to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges action against supplying Japan with oil, scrap iron, munitions or loans.
subfiles.summary: Stuart calls Japan's campaign an unjust attack on China, says American exports make the U.S. a partner, and argues cutting off supplies and credit would end it.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Senator Byrd
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Stuart’s letter and sends Byrd the Department’s reply and enclosures.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Byrd Stuart raised oil, scrap and munitions shipments, encloses the reply to Stuart and returns Stuart's letter.

subfiles.title: Reply to Warren Horton Stuart on exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory limits on stopping exports to Japan and reiterates official condemnation of bombing civilians.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Stuart the Neutrality Act would halt arms to both China and Japan but not oil or scrap, gives license totals, cites Hull's June 11 condemnation of civilian bombing, and says the government will keep discouraging inhumane conduct.

subfiles.title: Sam Silver’s request for names of aircraft exporters to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests public identification of private corporations exporting warplanes and aircraft parts to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sam Silver welcomes Hull's June 11 statement against supplying aircraft for indiscriminate bombing and asks the Department to name corporations shipping planes and parts to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Sam Silver on confidential export-license details
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Declines to identify individual aircraft exporters while providing aggregate munitions-control publications.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Silver for supporting the government’s position on civilian bombing but refuses to disclose the names of individual exporters. He explains that the Department publishes monthly aggregate licensing statements while withholding individual license details, and encloses an annual report and the May 1938 press statement.

subfiles.title: Robert J. Bulkley’s forwarding letter concerning Miriam Rogers
subfiles.about: Forwards Miriam Rogers’s letter urging cessation of arms shipments to Japan and requests a comment for her.
subfiles.summary: Robert Bulkley sends Hull Miriam Rogers's Warren, Ohio letter and asks a State comment to pass on.

subfiles.title: Miriam Rogers’s appeal to stop war-material shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges an end to American shipments of arms and all other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rogers appeals on humanity, Christianity and self-interest, warning that helping Japan defeat China would arm a rival and threaten the Open Door.

subfiles.title: Memorandum requesting approval of the draft reply to Bulkley
subfiles.about: Calls Hull’s attention to proposed written use of his June 11 remarks condemning civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Division notes no written account of Hull's June 11 press statements yet exists; since the draft may be reused in many replies, it seeks his approval first.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to Senator Bulkley concerning Miriam Rogers
subfiles.about: Provides a suggested explanation of the Neutrality Act and Hull’s condemnation of civilian bombing for transmission to Rogers.
subfiles.summary: The draft says a presidential proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan, while no authority existed to single out Japan. It supplies comparative export-license totals and recounts Hull’s June 11 statement condemning attacks on civilians and the material encouragement of such attacks. Rogers’s original letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Italian aircraft and ammunition supplied to Japan
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes military-attaché reporting on Italian bombers, artillery components and aviation personnel connected with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: Japan contracted for 200 BR.20 bombers and 200 spare engines, at least 112 shipped; a Borgomanero plant makes projectile cases for Japan; Italian aviation personnel apparently went as civilians, and most of the Italian mission in China went home.

subfiles.title: Military attaché report on Italian assistance to Japan
subfiles.doc_type: military intelligence report with routing sheet
subfiles.from: George N. Paine, Military Attaché, Rome
subfiles.about: Reports Italian aircraft shipments, ammunition production and aviation personnel associated with Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Paine reports a contract for 200 Italian bombers and spare engines, four planes numbered 109-112 crated at Marina di Pisa, projectile cases from Borgomanero, and unlikely combat service by Italian airmen, who may be civilian instructors.

subfiles.title: Continued Expansion of Armament Industry
subfiles.from: John K. Emmerson, American Vice Consul, approved by George A. Makinson
subfiles.to: Supervising Consul General, Tokyo, and Department of State
subfiles.about: Analyzes the expansion of Japanese munitions production and the conversion of smaller industries to armament work.
subfiles.summary: The report compares orders and production capacity at major Japanese manufacturers, showing that demand for war materials greatly exceeded existing output despite rapid factory expansion. It describes government subsidies, technical supervision, industrial guilds and factory pooling intended to convert small and medium firms to munitions production while addressing shortages of capital, skilled labor and technical knowledge. Examples show civilian manufacturers abandoning ordinary products for military equipment, and the conclusion argues that effective armament production could determine the survival of Japan’s small-industry system.

subfiles.title: Telephone memorandum on planned Washington peace delegation
subfiles.about: Reports plans for a delegation demanding prohibition of war-supply shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Miss Loomis relays a telegram: peace societies and church groups plan to come to Washington to press for banning war supplies to Japan, coordinated by Earl Leaf's New York information exchange.

subfiles.title: Edward H. Hume’s telegram supporting an embargo
subfiles.about: Supports State Department pressure on aviation manufacturers and calls for a complete embargo on war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Edward Hume approves pressure on aviation-material manufacturers and says he telegraphed the President and Hull supporting China-relief groups seeking a full embargo.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck’s acknowledgment to Edward H. Hume
subfiles.about: Acknowledges and appreciates Hume’s supportive telegram.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck cordially thanks Hume for his June 13 message without addressing the embargo.

subfiles.title: Further report on Japanese military commandeering of trucks
subfiles.about: Supplies additional reports of used trucks commandeered by Japanese military authorities.
subfiles.summary: Boyce reports further seizures of trucks in several Japanese localities, including Yokohama, Chiba and Tokyo. The clearest figure states that roughly 1,000 used trucks had recently been commandeered in Tokyo. Copies were distributed to the embassy, State Department, consulate general and military attaché.

subfiles.title: Edward H. Hume’s letter urging pressure on exporters to Japan
subfiles.about: Advocates category-by-category pressure on manufacturers exporting vehicles, fuel and aviation materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Edward Hume cites bombing of American property and Japan's attempt to define a Chinese war zone, notes fears Japan might declare war to trigger neutrality laws, and argues State pressure could persuade manufacturers to curtail strategic exports.

subfiles.title: Reply to Edward H. Hume on war-material exports
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the Neutrality Act’s limits and directs Hume to Hull’s statement on sales of aeronautical equipment.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Hume a proclamation would bar arms to both China and Japan, no law allows embargoing Japan alone or non-munitions goods, and the President judged invocation contrary to U.S. interests; license totals given, with Hull's June 11 aircraft remarks.

subfiles.title: Tom Connally’s forwarding note to the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent communication for favorable consideration and requests a report.
subfiles.summary: Tom Connally forwards an enclosure to State and asks it to report its disposition and return the letter.

subfiles.title: Nellie M. Broderson’s appeal against sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges Connally to stop sales of bombing planes and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Nellie Broderson condemns American sales contributing to the destruction of defenseless Chinese civilians, contrasting them with charity appeals as inconsistent and greedy.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Senator Connally
subfiles.about: Provides materials and an explanation of the Neutrality Act for transmission to Broderson.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Connally a proclamation would halt arms to both China and Japan, there's no authority for a unilateral embargo, gives license totals and his June 11 condemnation of civilian bombing, and encloses a pamphlet, the resolution and Broderson's letter.

subfiles.title: Nathan Alexander’s appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Asks Roosevelt to stop American war-material sales to Japan after attacks on Chinese civilian centers.
subfiles.summary: Alexander cites news photographs and reports of Japanese bombing and asks how the United States can continue furnishing war materials. He asserts that decisive presidential action would be popular and supported by the country.

subfiles.title: Reply to Nathan Alexander on exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked and why it could not prohibit ordinary commodities.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Nathan Alexander a war proclamation would embargo arms to both countries, no authority exists to bar Japan alone or non-listed commodities, and the President judged invocation contrary to U.S. interests; license totals and pamphlet enclosed.

subfiles.title: Chevy Chase Presbyterian Church telegram to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Arthur T. Pienkowsky, for the Session of Chevy Chase Presbyterian Church
subfiles.about: Supports official condemnation of bombing civilians and opposes current war-supply shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Chevy Chase Presbyterian Church session telegraphs Hull, backing the condemnation of bombing civilians and condemning continued war-supply shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: White House referral of the Chevy Chase Presbyterian Church telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards the church’s duplicate telegram condemning civilian bombing and war-supply exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: White House referral copy of the Chevy Chase Presbyterian telegram supporting condemnation of civilian attacks and opposing war-material shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Arthur T. Pienkowsky and the Chevy Chase Presbyterian Church
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges both copies of the church telegram and explains the government’s Neutrality Act position.
subfiles.summary: Green thanks Arthur Pienkowsky and the church, explaining the Neutrality Act would embargo China as well as Japan, ordinary commodities are outside it, and the President declined to invoke it; license figures, resolution and pamphlet enclosed.
